```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(DeCovarT)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE
)
```

DeCovarT estimates a composition $\boldsymbol{p}\in\Delta^{J-1}$ by
maximising the Gaussian-convolution log-likelihood

$$
\ell_{\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{\zeta}}(\boldsymbol{p})
=
-\tfrac{1}{2}\log\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})
-\tfrac{1}{2}
(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})^{\top}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})^{-1}
(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})
+C,
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})=\sum_{j=1}^{J}p_j^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j .
$$ {#eq-loglik}

The model, its ILR parametrisation and the derivatives of @eq-loglik
are in the
[population generative and optimisation vignette](01-1-population-generative-optimisation.html).
The single-cell counterpart of this vignette, with the two technical
scales profiled out, is the
[single-cell inference vignette](02-2-single-cell-inference.html).
This vignette asks three questions.

1. **What is the estimator entitled to claim?** The
   [generative vignette](01-1-population-generative-optimisation.html#sec-naive-model)
   fixes the parametrisation; @sec-mle-properties gives identifiability,
   existence, the failure of concavity and the finite-sample bias, and
   @sec-fisher-wald the expected Fisher information that every Wald
   interval uses.
2. **How should uncertainty on the proportions be reported?**
   @sec-intervals states the regularity conditions of the large-sample
   approximation, reads the local geometry of the log-likelihood,
   compares the Wald, likelihood-ratio and score tests and inverts them
   into intervals, maps intervals from the unconstrained coordinate
   $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ to $\boldsymbol{p}$, and treats nuisance scales,
   higher-order corrections, the finite-sample devices (Firth
   penalisation, the sandwich) and what conformal calibration can and
   cannot certify. @sec-inference covers likelihood ratios on the
   boundary and the bootstraps.
3. **Which model should be fitted to real data?** @sec-glm argues for
   modelling the conditional mean through a link rather than
   transforming the data, writes DeCovarT as a multivariate
   quasi-likelihood model, and ends with the recommended model for a
   single UMI reference and few bulk samples (@sec-final-choice).

Two facts frame everything below: the realised log-likelihood is **not**
concave and its maximiser **need not be unique**, and every Wald-type
interval is **undefined** on a simplex face. Their remedies are
implemented in [`lrt_decovart()`](../reference/lrt_decovart.html),
[`confint_profile_decovart()`](../reference/confint_profile_decovart.html),
[`bootstrap_decovart()`](../reference/bootstrap_decovart.html) and
[`reference_bootstrap_decovart()`](../reference/reference_bootstrap_decovart.html).

{{< include _notation.qmd >}}

# Theoretical properties of the DeCovarT MLE {#sec-mle-properties}

## Identifiability {#sec-identifiability}

::: {#prp-identifiability}
## Identifiability of the composition

The parameter-to-distribution map is

$$
\boldsymbol{p}
\longmapsto
\bigl(
  \boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p},\;
  \boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})
  =\textstyle\sum_{j}p_{j}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}
\bigr).
$$ {#eq-param-map}

Two compositions induce the same law
$\mathcal{N}_G(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p},
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p}))$ only if they coincide, **provided that
map is injective**. Full column rank of $\boldsymbol{\mu}$
($\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol{\mu})=J$, equivalently linearly
independent contrast columns
$\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot J}$) is a convenient
**sufficient** condition, because then the mean map alone is injective on
the simplex. It is **not necessary**. Two cell types may share identical
or collinear mean profiles and remain identifiable when their covariances
differ: the second component of @eq-param-map still separates
$\boldsymbol{p}$. Conversely, identical means *and* proportional
covariances ($\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{2}=c\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{1}$) make the
Gaussian family non-injective.
:::

Identifiability is a property of the *reference*, not of the bulk sample:
no amount of sequencing rescues a pair of types that agree in both mean
and covariance. The mean-based condition number $\kappa(\boldsymbol{\mu})$
is therefore a misleading diagnostic in the covariance-only regime
DeCovarT targets (see the
[feature-selection vignette](03-1-feature-selection.html#sec-weighted-kappa)).
Near-collinear *means* are still reported as a warning by
[`fit_decovart()`](../reference/fit_decovart.html); that warning does not
by itself imply that $\boldsymbol{p}$ is unidentifiable. Numerical
illustrations live in the
[appendix simulations](S1-identifiability.html).


## Existence {#sec-existence}

::: {#prp-existence}
## Existence of a maximiser

If every $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ is symmetric positive definite, then
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})=\sum_j p_j^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$
is positive definite for every $\boldsymbol{p}\in\Delta^{J-1}$, since at
least one $p_j>0$ on the simplex. Hence @eq-loglik is finite and
continuous on the **compact** set $\Delta^{J-1}$, and attains its
supremum.
:::

Two practical consequences. First, positive definiteness is preserved
even when some proportions are exactly zero, which is what allows the
restricted maximisation of
[`restricted_mle_decovart()`](../reference/restricted_mle_decovart.html)
to represent a null such as $p_j=0$ exactly instead of pushing it through
a logarithm. Second, the maximiser may lie on the **boundary** of the
compact set, so first-order conditions $\nabla\ell=\boldsymbol{0}$ are
necessary only at interior optima.

## Uniqueness fails for one observed sample {#sec-uniqueness}

Existence is not uniqueness. The DeCovarT likelihood is a
*heteroscedastic* Gaussian model: the noise covariance depends on the
same parameter as the mean, so @eq-loglik is not the concave objective of
an ordinary linear regression. Even in the isotropic case
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2=\mathbf{I}_G$ with $J=2$ and
without the simplex constraint,

$$
\ell(\boldsymbol{p})
=
-\frac{G}{2}\log(p_1^{2}+p_2^{2})
-
\frac{\lVert\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}\rVert^{2}}
{2(p_1^{2}+p_2^{2})}
+C ,
$$ {#eq-isotropic}

whose variance term moves with the coefficients. A single evaluation of
the analytic Hessian settles the question.

```{r}
#| label: nonconcavity
mean_signature <- matrix(c(2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 6 / 5), nrow = 3)
colnames(mean_signature) <- c("ct1", "ct2")
rownames(mean_signature) <- paste0("gene_", 1:3)
Sigma_iso <- array(c(diag(3), diag(3)), dim = c(3, 3, 2))
bulk <- drop(mean_signature %*% c(0.5, 0.5))

hessian_interior <- hessian_loglik_unconstrained(
  p = c(1 / 5, 3 / 10),
  y = bulk,
  mean_signature_matrix = mean_signature,
  Sigma = Sigma_iso
)
round(hessian_interior, 4)
c(
  determinant = det(hessian_interior),
  eigen(hessian_interior, symmetric = TRUE)$values
)
```

Every entry of $\boldsymbol{y}$ and $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ is strictly
positive, $\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol{\mu})=2$, $G=3>J=2$, and both
covariances are positive definite. Yet the Hessian at the strictly
interior point $\boldsymbol{p}=(1/5,3/10)$ has one positive and one
negative eigenvalue.

::: {#nte-nonconcave .callout-important}
## One indefinite Hessian disproves global concavity

A negative determinant at a single admissible point is a counterexample,
so the unconstrained DeCovarT log-likelihood is **not globally concave**
under the stated positivity and rank assumptions. The same conclusion
transfers to the isometric log-ratio chart, because a $C^{2}$
diffeomorphism preserves the existence of directions of positive
curvature. Consequently:

- a converged optimiser certifies a **local** maximum at best;
- several starts may reach different modes (see @sec-diagnostics);
- convex-optimisation guarantees — a unique global optimum reachable by
  descent, and duality certificates — do not apply
  [@boydConvexOptimization2004]. The step safeguards of second-order
  solvers, the Newton trust region of `nlminb` and the Marquardt–Levenberg
  damping of `marqLevAlg` [@R-marqLevAlg; @philippsRobustEfficientOptimization2021],
  and the relative-distance-to-minimum criterion of
  @commengesNewtonLikeAlgorithmLikelihood2006 buy robustness against
  saddle points, not global optimality.
:::

## Population consistency and efficiency {#sec-population}

The failure of concavity is a statement about *one realised* data set.
The population criterion behaves much better. Let $\boldsymbol{p}_0$ be
the truth and define
$Q(\boldsymbol{p};\boldsymbol{p}_0)
=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{p}_0}\{\ell_{\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{p})\}$.

::: {#thm-population}
## Population uniqueness through the Kullback–Leibler divergence

$$
Q(\boldsymbol{p}_0;\boldsymbol{p}_0)-Q(\boldsymbol{p};\boldsymbol{p}_0)
=
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(
  P_{\boldsymbol{p}_0}\,\Vert\,P_{\boldsymbol{p}}
\bigr)
\ \ge\ 0 ,
$$ {#eq-kl}

with equality if and only if
$P_{\boldsymbol{p}}=P_{\boldsymbol{p}_0}$. Under
@prp-identifiability that happens only at
$\boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{p}_0$, so $\boldsymbol{p}_0$ is the
**unique** maximiser of the expected log-likelihood.
:::

@eq-kl is an identifiability statement, not a curvature statement: it
survives the non-concavity of @nte-nonconcave. It is also the engine of
the usual asymptotics — consistency, asymptotic normality and efficiency
of the MLE [@vaartAsymptoticStatistics2000] — because the local geometry
of the divergence *is* the Fisher information. By the
[Fisher information metric theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence#Fisher_information_metric_theorem),

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(
  P_{\boldsymbol{p}_0}\,\Vert\,P_{\boldsymbol{p}_0+\boldsymbol{d}}
\bigr)
=
\tfrac{1}{2}\,
\boldsymbol{d}^{\top}I(\boldsymbol{p}_0)\,\boldsymbol{d}
+
o(\lVert\boldsymbol{d}\rVert^{2}) ,
$$ {#eq-fisher-metric}

with $I$ the expected information of
[`expected_fisher_unconstrained()`](../reference/expected_fisher_unconstrained.html);
the Gaussian case is treated in information-geometric terms by
@malagoInformationGeometryGaussian2015. The identity is worth checking
numerically, since it ties the plug-in `vcov` of a DeCovarT fit to the
divergence that makes the MLE consistent.

```{r}
#| label: kl-fisher
kl_gaussian_convolution <- function(p_ref, p_alt, mu, Sigma) {
  mean_ref <- drop(mu %*% p_ref)
  mean_alt <- drop(mu %*% p_alt)
  cov_ref <- .compute_global_variance(p_ref, Sigma)
  cov_alt <- .compute_global_variance(p_alt, Sigma)
  precision_alt <- solve(cov_alt)
  shift <- mean_alt - mean_ref
  0.5 *
    (sum(diag(precision_alt %*% cov_ref)) -
      nrow(cov_ref) +
      drop(t(shift) %*% precision_alt %*% shift) +
      as.numeric(determinant(cov_alt, logarithm = TRUE)$modulus) -
      as.numeric(determinant(cov_ref, logarithm = TRUE)$modulus))
}

p_reference <- c(0.4, 0.6)
information <- expected_fisher_unconstrained(
  p_reference,
  mean_signature,
  Sigma_iso
)
steps <- c(1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4)
data.frame(
  step = steps,
  kullback_leibler = vapply(
    steps,
    function(h) {
      kl_gaussian_convolution(
        p_reference,
        p_reference + c(h, -h / 2),
        mean_signature,
        Sigma_iso
      )
    },
    numeric(1)
  ),
  quadratic_form = vapply(
    steps,
    function(h) {
      d <- c(h, -h / 2)
      0.5 * drop(t(d) %*% information %*% d)
    },
    numeric(1)
  )
)
```

The two columns agree to the order of $\lVert\boldsymbol{d}\rVert^{3}$,
as @eq-fisher-metric predicts.

## Finite-sample bias versus asymptotic unbiasedness {#sec-finite-sample}

@thm-population is a statement about the *expected* criterion
$Q(\boldsymbol{p};\boldsymbol{p}_0)$. It does not say that the maximiser of
one realised log-likelihood equals $\boldsymbol{p}_0$. Typical bulk
deconvolution observes a single $G$-vector
$\boldsymbol{Y}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathcal{N}_G(\boldsymbol{\mu}
\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}))$
and treats that column as $N=1$. The resulting MLE is then a nonlinear
function of one Gaussian draw, so
$\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{p}_0}(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})\neq\boldsymbol{p}_0$
in general: the leading bias of a regular MLE is $O(N^{-1})$
[@vaartAsymptoticStatistics2000, Ch. 5]. The same map becomes consistent,
and $\sqrt{N}$-normal with variance $I(\boldsymbol{p}_0)^{-1}$, once
$N$ i.i.d. bulk columns share one composition, because the averaged
criterion converges to $Q$ and $Q$ has a unique maximiser at
$\boldsymbol{p}_0$.

Two calculations are easy to confuse and are not the same.

**Score identity.** If the convolution is correctly specified,
$\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{p}_0}\{\nabla\ell_{\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{p}_0)\}=\boldsymbol{0}$.
The identity is a property of the *random* bulk. It is what the Fisher
metric of @eq-fisher-metric linearises.

**Mean-profile remainder.** Substituting the *conditional mean*
$\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}_0$ into the score of @eq-loglik
kills the Mahalanobis terms and leaves only the derivative of
$-\tfrac12\log\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})$. In unconstrained
$\boldsymbol{p}$-coordinates that remainder is
$-p_j\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\Omega}(\boldsymbol{p})
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\bigr)$ at each $j$, with
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})^{-1}$. Mapped through
the ILR chart it vanishes by symmetry when
$\boldsymbol{p}_0=(1/2,1/2)$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2$,
and it does **not** vanish at an unbalanced interior point. Hence the
maximiser of $\ell(\,\cdot\,;\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}_0)$ need not equal
$\boldsymbol{p}_0$ even though that bulk sits at the centre of the
model. The bias of the *random* MLE is a different, typically larger,
effect: $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$ is a nonlinear function of $\boldsymbol{Y}$,
and near a simplex face the ILR chart sends $p_j\to 0$ to
$|\rho|\to\infty$ so that a plateau in $\ell$ (see @sec-boundary)
inflates the $O(N^{-1})$ term.

Convex-optimisation guarantees do not close the gap. Boyd and
Vandenberghe emphasise that a local maximum of a non-concave objective
need not be global, and that first-order stationarity certifies
optimality only under convexity
[@boydConvexOptimization2004, Ch. 1 and 4]. @nte-nonconcave already
exhibits an indefinite Hessian for one bulk, so a converged solver
certifies a *local* maximiser of that sample's $\ell$, not uniqueness
and not unbiasedness. What *is* uniquely maximised is $Q$, and only
after $N\to\infty$ (or after pooling genuine replicates; @sec-replication)
does $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_N$ concentrate there.

```{r}
#| label: finite-sample-score
mu_cld <- matrix(c(20, 22, 22, 20), nrow = 2)
Sigma_id <- array(c(diag(2), diag(2)), dim = c(2, 2, 2))
p_balanced <- c(0.5, 0.5)
p_rare <- c(0.99, 0.01)
y_at_mean <- function(p) {
  drop(mu_cld %*% p)
}
score_at_mean <- function(p) {
  gradient_loglik_constrained(
    isometric_log_ratio(p),
    y_at_mean(p),
    mu_cld,
    Sigma_id
  )
}
set.seed(1)
cov_rare <- .compute_global_variance(p_rare, Sigma_id)
mean_score_random <- mean(replicate(200, {
  y <- MASS::mvrnorm(
    n = 1,
    mu = y_at_mean(p_rare),
    Sigma = cov_rare
  )
  gradient_loglik_constrained(
    isometric_log_ratio(p_rare),
    y,
    mu_cld,
    Sigma_id
  )
}))
data.frame(
  composition = c("balanced 50-50", "rare type 0.01"),
  ilr_score_at_conditional_mean = c(
    score_at_mean(p_balanced),
    score_at_mean(p_rare)
  ),
  mean_ilr_score_at_truth = c(NA_real_, mean_score_random)
)
```

The ILR score at the conditional mean is zero in the balanced isotropic
case and of order $10^{-2}$ at $p=(0.99,0.01)$. Averaging the same score
over random $\boldsymbol{Y}\sim\mathcal{N}_G(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}_0,
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p}_0))$ returns a number consistent with
zero, as the information identity requires. Finite-sample bias of
$\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$ is therefore not a failure of
$\mathbb{E}(\nabla\ell)=0$; it is the nonlinearity of the maximiser,
amplified when @eq-loglik is nearly flat along a simplex face. The
bivariate and covariance-driven Monte Carlo packs in
`output/fig02/mle_explanation/` and `output/fig03/mle_explanation/`
quantify that geometry for $N=1$ (see
[the bivariate toy](R1-bivariate-toy.html#sec-bivariate-findings) and
[the covariance-driven scenario](R2-covariance-driven.html#sec-hybrid-findings)).
A Jeffreys / Firth adjustment of $\ell$
[@firthBiasReductionMaximum1993] shrinks the $O(N^{-1})$ term when
replicates are scarce (@sec-firth).

## Equivariance: affine yes, logarithmic no {#sec-equivariance}

::: {#prp-equivariance}
## Gene-wise affine equivariance

Let $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\operatorname{diag}(\varsigma_1,\ldots,\varsigma_G)$ with $\varsigma_g\neq 0$ and
$\boldsymbol{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{G}$. Applying the **same** gene-wise map to
all three inputs,

$$
\boldsymbol{y}^{\star}=\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{t}),
\quad
\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\star}
=\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\mu}-\boldsymbol{t}\mathbf{1}_J^{\top}),
\quad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j^{\star}=\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1},
$$

leaves the MLE unchanged, because $\mathbf{1}_J^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}=1$
makes the recentring cancel and the Mahalanobis residual is invariant.
:::

A z-score computed **once per gene from $\boldsymbol{\mu}$** is such a
map, which is why `fit_decovart(standardise = TRUE)` is safe. Per-cell-type
or per-sample scaling is not, and neither is a logarithm: $\log$ is
concave, so Jensen's inequality shifts both moments and
$\log(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})
\neq(\log\boldsymbol{\mu})\boldsymbol{p}$. Reference-based deconvolution
therefore expects a non-log linear scale
[@newmanRobustEnumerationCell2015]: **keep raw counts** (or a linear
normalisation such as CPM/TPM) rather than $\log_2$ values. Monotonicity
of $\log$ preserves gene-wise rankings, but not the convolution MLE. The
numerical demonstration lives in the
[appendix simulations](S1-identifiability.html#sec-affine).

# Expected Fisher information and Wald inference {#sec-fisher-wald}

Point estimation alone does not report uncertainty. Under a regular
large-sample regime the MLE is asymptotically normal with covariance
given by the inverse Fisher information. DeCovarT builds Wald standard
errors from the *expected* Fisher information of the multivariate-normal
convolution, then maps that information through the ILR chart.

## Unconstrained expected Fisher information {#sec-fisher-p}

For
$\boldsymbol{y}\sim\mathcal{N}_{G}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p},
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})\bigr)$ the expected Fisher information
has entries

$$
I(\boldsymbol{p})_{j\ell}
=
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}^{\top}
\boldsymbol{\Omega}(\boldsymbol{p})
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot \ell}
+
2p_{j}p_{\ell}\,
\mathrm{tr}\bigl(
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}(\boldsymbol{p})\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}
  \boldsymbol{\Omega}(\boldsymbol{p})\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}
\bigr).
$$ {#eq-fisher-p}

The first summand is the mean contribution (a $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$-inner
product of signature columns); the second is the covariance contribution
of the quadratic map
$\boldsymbol{p}\mapsto\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})$. See the
multivariate-normal formula on
[Wikipedia: Fisher information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_information#Multivariate_normal_distribution).
[`expected_fisher_unconstrained()`](../reference/expected_fisher_unconstrained.html)
implements @eq-fisher-p.

::: {#nte-obs-vs-exp .callout-note}
## Observed versus expected information

The analytic Hessian of the
[unconstrained score and Hessian](01-1-population-generative-optimisation.html#sec-unconstrained) is the *observed* information
(up to sign). Wald intervals in `decovart_fit` use the *expected*
information @eq-fisher-p, which does not depend on the residual
$\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}$ and is positive definite under
the usual full-rank assumptions on $(\boldsymbol{\mu},\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}\})$.

The two are consistent by construction. Substituting
$\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{r}]=\boldsymbol{0}$ and
$\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{r}\boldsymbol{r}^{\top}]
=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})$ into the
[diagonal](01-1-population-generative-optimisation.html#eq-hess-diag) and
[off-diagonal](01-1-population-generative-optimisation.html#eq-hess-off)
Hessian entries cancels the determinant traces against the residual
traces and returns @eq-fisher-p exactly, i.e.
$\mathbb{E}[-\mathbf{H}]=I(\boldsymbol{p})$. That identity only holds with
the factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ on the
[determinant term](01-1-population-generative-optimisation.html#nte-halfdet) in place.
:::

## Constrained case: ILR delta method {#sec-fisher-rho}

Fisher information transforms as a covariant quadratic form under the
ILR chart. With the
[ILR Jacobian](01-1-population-generative-optimisation.html#sec-ilr-deriv)
$\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}=\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})\mathbf{V}$,

$$
I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}
=
\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}^{\mathsf{T}}
I(\boldsymbol{p})
\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}
=
\mathbf{V}^{\mathsf{T}}
\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})
I(\boldsymbol{p})
\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})
\mathbf{V}.
$$ {#eq-fisher-rho}

The mean/covariance split of @eq-fisher-p pulls back separately,
$I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}=I_{\boldsymbol{\rho},\mathrm{mean}}
+I_{\boldsymbol{\rho},\mathrm{cov}}$. Under regularity,
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}
\overset{a}{\sim}
\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\rho}_{0},I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}^{-1})$
[@vaartAsymptoticStatistics2000].
The first-order delta method [@oehlertNoteDeltaMethod1992] then returns
the simplex covariance used by
[`vcov.decovart_fit()`](../reference/fit_decovart.html),

$$
\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})
\approx
\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}
I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}^{-1}
\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}^{\mathsf{T}}.
$$ {#eq-delta-p}

Diagonal square roots are asymptotic standard errors; Wald intervals at
level $1-\alpha$ are
$\hat{p}_{j}\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\mathrm{SE}_{j}$ with
$z_{q}=\Phi^{-1}(q)$, as in
[`confint.decovart_fit()`](../reference/fit_decovart.html).
[`vcov_ilr_delta()`](../reference/vcov_ilr_delta.html) implements
@eq-fisher-rho--@eq-delta-p. Orthogonal rotations of $\mathbf{V}$ leave
@eq-delta-p unchanged. The construction is undefined on the simplex
boundary (the log-ratio chart blows up); the helper then returns `NA`
with a warning.

::: {#nte-wald-limits .callout-warning}
## Wald is the cheapest, not the safest, interval

@eq-delta-p linearises the ILR chart at $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$, so it is
neither invariant to a non-orthogonal reparametrisation nor confined to
$[0,1]$, and it degenerates entirely when a proportion reaches a simplex
face. @sec-intervals and @sec-inference derive the alternatives: profile likelihood-ratio intervals, the
chi-bar-square calibration of Chernoff and of Self and Liang for nulls on
the boundary, a parametric bootstrap, and a reference-sample bootstrap
of donors or cells (or a Dirichlet composition sweep). It also shows why
these limits need replicate samples that share one composition.
Shuffling genes or cell-type names of an averaged signature is not a
bootstrap: the maximised likelihood is equivariant under relabelling.
:::

# Confidence intervals for the proportions {#sec-intervals}

The solver returns $\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ and an information matrix in
$\boldsymbol{\rho}$-coordinates,
$I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}=\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}^{\top}I(\boldsymbol{p})\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}$
with $\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}=\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})\mathbf{V}$
(@sec-fisher-rho).
This section follows the generalised-linear-model treatment of
likelihood inference [@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015,
Sects. 4.2--4.3]: state when the large-sample approximation holds
(@sec-regularity), read the local geometry of the log-likelihood
(@sec-geometry), define the three first-order tests (@sec-three-tests),
and invert them into intervals (@sec-test-inversion). The remaining
subsections treat the routes from $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ to $\boldsymbol{p}$,
nuisance scales, and corrections beyond first order.

## Regularity conditions and two asymptotic regimes {#sec-regularity}

::: {#prp-regularity}
## Large-sample normality and the three first-order tests

Let $\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot 1},\ldots,\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot N}$ be independent
bulk profiles of $N$ biological samples that share one composition
$\boldsymbol{p}_0$, and write
$\boldsymbol{\rho}_0=\mathbf{V}^{\top}\log\boldsymbol{p}_0$. Assume that

- **(R1) identifiability:** distinct compositions give distinct laws
  (@prp-identifiability);
- **(R2) interior truth:** $\boldsymbol{p}_0$ lies in the open simplex, so
  $\boldsymbol{\rho}_0$ is a finite point of the open set
  $\mathbb{R}^{J-1}$;
- **(R3) fixed dimension:** the number of free parameters $J-1$, and the
  number of genes $G$, stay fixed while $N\to\infty$;
- **(R4) smoothness:** the log-density is three times continuously
  differentiable in $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ near $\boldsymbol{\rho}_0$, with third
  derivatives bounded by an integrable function;
- **(R5) information:** the per-sample Fisher information
  $I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(\boldsymbol{\rho}_0)$ is finite and positive definite;
- **(R6) fixed support:** the support of the law does not depend on
  $\boldsymbol{\rho}$, and differentiation and integration can be
  interchanged.

Then, with probability tending to one, the likelihood equation has a
consistent root $\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$, and

$$
\sqrt{N}\,(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}-\boldsymbol{\rho}_0)
\ \rightsquigarrow\
\mathcal{N}_{J-1}\bigl(\boldsymbol{0},I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}(\boldsymbol{\rho}_0)^{-1}\bigr).
$$ {#eq-asymptotic-normality}

For a null hypothesis that fixes $k$ smooth functions of
$\boldsymbol{\rho}$, the Wald, likelihood-ratio and score statistics of
@sec-three-tests all converge to $\chi^{2}_{k}$ and differ by $o_P(1)$
[@coxTheoreticalStatistics1979, Sects. 9.2--9.3].
:::

The Gaussian convolution meets (R4) and (R6) on the open simplex,
because $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})$ is positive definite on the closed
simplex (@sec-existence). The other conditions are where DeCovarT can
fail.

- **(R5)** fails when two signature columns are collinear and the
  covariances do not separate the types: the information is singular
  along their contrast.
- **(R2)** fails when a type is absent. The limit is then the
  chi-bar-square mixture of @sec-boundary, not a Gaussian.
- **(R3)** fixes the direction of the limit. The replication unit is the
  biological sample $i$, not the gene: the $G$ genes are correlated by
  construction, and their dependence through $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})$
  is the point of the model. A design that gives every new sample its own
  composition adds parameters as fast as observations, so no single
  composition gains information [@coxTheoreticalStatistics1979, p. 81].
  @sec-replication draws the practical consequences.

**Small-dispersion asymptotics.** @prp-regularity needs replicates. A
single bulk sample still has an asymptotic direction under the
single-cell model of @eq-final-model: with
$\tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}_{\cdot i}=\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}/c_i$,

$$
\tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}_{\cdot i}\sim
\mathcal{N}_G\bigl(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i},\;
n_i^{-1}\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})\bigr),
$$ {#eq-small-dispersion}

so the number of cells $n_i$ plays the role of the index parameter
of a dispersion model, and $1/n_i$ that of the dispersion.
For a **single** observation from a dispersion model,
@jørgensenSmallDispersionAsymptotics1987 proves consistency, the limit
$n_i^{1/2}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\boldsymbol{\beta}_0)\rightsquigarrow
\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},i(\boldsymbol{\beta}_0)^{-1})$, and $\chi^{2}$ limits
for differences of deviances, as the index $n_i\to\infty$ with the sample size
fixed (his Theorems 4.1--4.3). His conditions mirror (R2), (R4) and
(R5): an open parameter set, a full-rank local design matrix and a
positive-definite information. Large expected counts in contingency
tables are the classical special case. Five points carry this result to
DeCovarT.

1. **Not exactly a dispersion model (our remark).** In
   @eq-small-dispersion the term
   $-\tfrac12\log\det\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})$ is not multiplied by
   $n_i$. It is $O(1)$ against the $O(n_i)$ Mahalanobis term, so the
   information is dominated by its mean part,
   $n_i\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}^{\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{S}_W^{-1}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}$,
   and the quasi-score of @sec-decovart-glm becomes efficient in this
   limit. The proof still has to be written.
2. **Every type must grow.** The Gaussian law of the bulk is itself a
   central-limit approximation over the cells of each type, so the limit
   needs every count $m_{ji}=n_ip_{ji}$ to grow, not only $n_i$. A rare
   type with few cells breaks the approximation first.
3. **Unknown dispersion.** Jørgensen estimates the dispersion by the
   deviance divided by its degrees of freedom (his Sect. 4.5). Here that
   is the Pearson estimate $\hat\phi$ on $G-J$ degrees of freedom: $G$
   must exceed $J$ by a margin, and $t$ or $F$ quantiles replace normal
   and $\chi^{2}$ ones when $G-J$ is small.
4. **Reference error does not shrink.** The moments
   $(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j})$ come from $C_j$ cells.
   Their error does not decrease with $n_i$ and dominates once
   $n_i\gg C_j$, which `reference_bootstrap_decovart()` propagates
   (@sec-reference-bootstrap).
5. **The released model has no index.** The covariance
   $\sum_jp_j^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ of @eq-loglik does not scale with a
   number of cells, so only the replicate limit of @prp-regularity is
   available for it.

## Local geometry of the log-likelihood {#sec-geometry}

Every first-order interval reads the curvature at the estimate. Near
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$,

$$
\ell(\boldsymbol{\rho})-\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}})
\approx
-\tfrac12(\boldsymbol{\rho}-\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}})^{\top}
\boldsymbol{j}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}})
(\boldsymbol{\rho}-\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{j}=-\nabla^{2}_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\ell ,
$$ {#eq-quadratic-approx}

and a scalar Wald half-width is $z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\boldsymbol{j}^{-1/2}$. A
sharp peak gives a narrow interval, a plateau a wide one, and a ridge,
as along the contrast of two collinear signatures, an elongated
ellipse. The approximation is exact in one case: a Gaussian response
with identity link and known covariance has a log-likelihood that is a
second-degree polynomial in the coefficients. There the Wald,
likelihood-ratio and score statistics are equal, their $\chi^{2}$ law is
exact, and the symmetric interval is exact
[@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015, Sect. 4.3]. DeCovarT departs
from that case in three ways.

- **The covariance depends on the parameter.** $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})$
  enters the log-determinant and the Mahalanobis weights, so $\ell$ is
  not quadratic even in $\boldsymbol{p}$, where the mean is linear.
- **The chart is nonlinear.** The mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\psi}(\boldsymbol{\rho})$
  is not linear in $\boldsymbol{\rho}$.
- **Faces flatten the likelihood.** $p_j\to0$ sends $\rho$ to infinity,
  and $\ell$ levels off along that direction. With few replicates, an
  unbalanced composition or overlapping types, the profile is skewed and
  its plateau wide. The ILR slices of the
  [covariance-driven scenario](R2-covariance-driven.html#sec-hybrid-findings)
  show these ridges along the contrast of the two mean-collinear types.

The geometry is also a diagnostic of non-normality. Compare the Wald,
score and likelihood-ratio intervals for the same estimate, and plot the
signed root $r(\tau)$ of @eq-signed-root against the Wald pivot
$(\hat\tau-\tau)/\mathrm{SE}$: the two curves coincide when $\ell$ is
quadratic, and a curved $r(\tau)$ or a large gap between the three
intervals flags a non-Gaussian geometry. Ratios of the three statistics
also detect the Hauck--Donner effect [@yeeHauckDonnerEffectWald2022].

## Wald, likelihood-ratio and score tests {#sec-three-tests}

Partition $\boldsymbol{\vartheta}=(\boldsymbol{\tau},\boldsymbol{\eta})$ into $k$
parameters of interest and nuisance parameters (other proportions,
scales), test $H_0:\boldsymbol{\tau}=\boldsymbol{\tau}_0$, write
$\tilde{\boldsymbol{\vartheta}}_0=(\boldsymbol{\tau}_0,\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{\boldsymbol{\tau}_0})$
for the restricted estimate, and $I^{\tau\tau}$ for the $\boldsymbol{\tau}$
block of $I^{-1}$ [@coxTheoreticalStatistics1979, Sect. 9.3;
@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015, Sect. 4.3]:

$$
W=(\hat{\boldsymbol{\tau}}-\boldsymbol{\tau}_0)^{\top}
\{I^{\tau\tau}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\vartheta}})\}^{-1}
(\hat{\boldsymbol{\tau}}-\boldsymbol{\tau}_0),
\quad
\mathcal{D}=2\{\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{\vartheta}})-\ell(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\vartheta}}_0)\},
\quad
S=\boldsymbol{U}_{\tau}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\vartheta}}_0)^{\top}
I^{\tau\tau}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\vartheta}}_0)
\boldsymbol{U}_{\tau}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\vartheta}}_0).
$$ {#eq-three-tests}

| | Wald $W$ | Likelihood ratio $\mathcal{D}$ | Score $S$ |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Fits needed | unrestricted | both | restricted |
| Evaluated at | $\hat{\boldsymbol{\vartheta}}$ (curvature) | both (height) | $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\vartheta}}_0$ (slope) |
| Smooth reparametrisation | changes it | invariant | invariant (expected information) |
| Simplex face | undefined | chi-bar-square (@sec-boundary) | defined in $\boldsymbol{p}$ coordinates |
| Interval shape | symmetric | asymmetric | asymmetric |

: The three first-order tests. {#tbl-three-tests}

- **Rao's score test is the Lagrange-multiplier test.** At the
  restricted maximum, the multiplier of the constraint
  $\boldsymbol{\tau}=\boldsymbol{\tau}_0$ equals the score
  $\boldsymbol{U}_{\tau}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\vartheta}}_0)$, so the two names
  describe one statistic.
- **Linear constraints.** The likelihood ratio tests any nested
  hypothesis, including $k$ linear constraints
  $\boldsymbol{C}\boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{d}$, with $\mathcal{D}\rightsquigarrow\chi^{2}_k$.
  In a lineage-aware fit, the hypothesis that two child lines occur in
  the ratio $w_0$ measured in their parental line is
  $p_{c_1}-w_0(p_{c_1}+p_{c_2})=0$, one linear constraint. The
  restricted set is still a polytope, but the constraint is not linear in
  $\boldsymbol{\rho}$, so the restricted fit is done in $\boldsymbol{p}$.
- **Asymptotic equivalence.** Under @prp-regularity the three statistics
  differ by $o_P(1)$ [@coxTheoreticalStatistics1979, Sect. 9.3]. They
  disagree in finite samples exactly when the geometry of
  @sec-geometry is not quadratic.
- **The relative distance to the maximum is a score statistic.** The
  stopping rule of the Marquardt--Levenberg solver is
  $\mathrm{RDM}=m^{-1}\boldsymbol{U}(\boldsymbol{\vartheta}_k)^{\top}\boldsymbol{G}(\boldsymbol{\vartheta}_k)^{-1}\boldsymbol{U}(\boldsymbol{\vartheta}_k)$,
  with $\boldsymbol{G}$ an estimate of the variance of the score (outer
  products of individual scores in the robust-variance scoring
  algorithm, the Hessian in `marqLevAlg`). It is a score statistic for
  the null "the iterate $\boldsymbol{\vartheta}_k$ is the maximiser", divided by
  the number $m$ of parameters, and Commenges et al. note that inverting
  $\boldsymbol{U}^{\top}\boldsymbol{G}^{-1}\boldsymbol{U}\le\chi^{2}_{m,1-\alpha}$
  gives a confidence region
  [@commengesNewtonLikeAlgorithmLikelihood2006, pp. 10 and 13]. The
  difference with Rao's test is the null: a numerical statement about
  the iterate, not a scientific hypothesis on $\boldsymbol{p}$.

## Confidence intervals by test inversion {#sec-test-inversion}

A $(1-\alpha)$ confidence set is the set of null values that a
level-$\alpha$ test does not reject,
$\{\tau_0:T(\tau_0)\le\chi^{2}_{1,1-\alpha}\}$ for each statistic of
@eq-three-tests [@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015, Sect. 4.3].

- **Wald.** The information is evaluated once, at $\hat\tau$, so the
  set is the symmetric interval
  $\hat\tau\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\mathrm{SE}(\hat\tau)$.
- **Score.** The information is re-evaluated at each candidate $\tau_0$,
  so the interval is asymmetric. For a binomial proportion it is the
  Wilson interval [@wilsonProbableInferenceLaw1927]. The score is
  computed at the restricted fit only, which on the simplex can sit on a
  face.
- **Likelihood ratio.** $\mathcal{D}(\tau_0)$ is zero at $\hat\tau$ and grows on both
  sides, so $\{\tau_0:\mathcal{D}(\tau_0)\le\chi^{2}_{1,1-\alpha}\}$ has a lower and an
  upper endpoint, where the profile deviance crosses the cut-off on each
  side of $\hat\tau$. The $\chi^{2}_1$ test is two-sided because it squares
  the signed likelihood root

  $$
  r(\tau_0)=\operatorname{sign}(\hat\tau-\tau_0)\sqrt{\mathcal{D}(\tau_0)}
  \ \rightsquigarrow\ \mathcal{N}(0,1).
  $$ {#eq-signed-root}

  The lower limit solves $r(\tau_L)=z_{1-\alpha/2}$, the upper limit
  $r(\tau_U)=-z_{1-\alpha/2}$, and $z_{1-\alpha}$ gives one-sided limits. If
  $\mathcal{D}$ stays below the cut-off all the way to the face $p_j=0$, the lower
  limit is $0$.
- **Several parameters.** The joint region
  $\{\boldsymbol{\tau}_0:\mathcal{D}(\boldsymbol{\tau}_0)\le\chi^{2}_{k,1-\alpha}\}$, with the
  remaining proportions and the scales profiled out as nuisance
  parameters (@sec-nuisance), has simultaneous coverage.

Software. [`confint_profile_decovart()`](../reference/confint_profile_decovart.html)
inverts @eq-lrt for DeCovarT. For generalised linear models,
[`stats::confint()`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/stats/versions/3.6.2/topics/confint)
inverts the signed root of the profile, and
[`ProfileLikelihood`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ProfileLikelihood)
plots normalised profiles and likelihood support intervals for linear,
generalised linear and mixed models. Of the higher-order packages,
[`likelihoodAsy`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=likelihoodAsy)
computes $r$ and $r^{\ast}$ (@sec-higher-order) for any scalar function of
the parameters from a user-supplied log-likelihood and data simulator,
so it applies to DeCovarT with `simulate_bulk_mixture()`, whereas
[`cond`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=cond) is restricted to
logistic and log-linear models.

## From $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ to $\boldsymbol{p}$: delta method or back-transformation {#sec-wald-routes}

A Wald statement in $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ still has to be carried to the
proportions. Agresti's advice for fitted values applies: the delta
method gives their covariance, but an interval formed on the scale of
the linear predictor and mapped by the inverse link avoids the further
approximation [@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015, Sect. 4.2.5].

1. **Delta method on $\boldsymbol{p}$.** $\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})\approx\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}^{-1}\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}^{\top}$
   and $\hat p_j\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\mathrm{SE}_j$. This is the default of
   [`confint.decovart_fit()`](../reference/fit_decovart.html). It is
   symmetric, and nothing keeps its endpoints inside $[0,1]$.
2. **Back-transformation through the ILR chart.** A smooth, monotone map
   preserves quantiles. For $J=2$,
   $p_1=\operatorname{logistic}(\sqrt{2}\,\rho)$ is monotone, so
   $[\psi(\hat\rho-z\,\mathrm{SE}),\psi(\hat\rho+z\,\mathrm{SE})]$ has exactly the
   coverage of the interval for $\rho$, lies inside $(0,1)$ and is
   asymmetric around $\hat p_1$. For $J>2$ each $p_j$ depends on all
   $J-1$ coordinates, but the bijection $\boldsymbol{\psi}$ maps joint regions
   exactly, $\Pr(\boldsymbol{\rho}\in R)=\Pr\{\boldsymbol{p}\in\boldsymbol{\psi}(R)\}$.
   Marginal intervals are the quantiles of
   $\boldsymbol{p}^{(b)}=\boldsymbol{\psi}(\boldsymbol{\rho}^{(b)})$ with
   $\boldsymbol{\rho}^{(b)}\sim\mathcal{N}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}},I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}^{-1})$.
   Every draw is a composition, so the intervals lie inside $(0,1)$ and
   respect the sum-to-one constraint jointly; for $J=2$ they reduce to
   the endpoint map.

**Why not a multinomial logit renormalisation.** Three alternatives were
considered and are not kept.

- *The free softmax* of $J$ scores, the machine-learning form of the
  multinomial logit in Burakov's chapter ([PDF](burakov-logistic-regression.pdf)),
  is not identifiable: $\operatorname{softmax}(\boldsymbol{z}+t\mathbf{1})=\operatorname{softmax}(\boldsymbol{z})$,
  and its information is singular along $\mathbf{1}$.
- *The multinomial logit with a reference type* is the ALR chart. It is
  a linear transform of the ILR chart, so it gives the same estimate, the
  same likelihood ratio, the same delta-method covariance of
  $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$ and the same back-transformed regions
  ([chart invariance](01-1-population-generative-optimisation.html#sec-chart-choice)).
  The ILR chart is kept for its numerical invariance: gradient norms,
  damping and conditioning do not depend on a reference type.
- *A component-wise logit interval*, the delta method applied to
  $\operatorname{logit}\hat p_j$ with
  $\mathrm{SE}(\operatorname{logit}\hat p_j)=\mathrm{SE}(\hat p_j)/\{\hat p_j(1-\hat p_j)\}$,
  stacks a second delta method on the first and does not use the chart
  the model was fitted in.

The transformation guarantees the **bounds**, not the **coverage**: both
routes rest on the same normal approximation of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$.
The simulation below checks both on an unbalanced three-type mixture
with a rare type ($p_3=0.03$), refitting DeCovarT on independent bulk
draws of one composition.

```{r}
#| label: interval-routes
#| warning: false
set.seed(2026)
n_genes <- 8L
n_types <- 3L
n_rep <- 300L
mu_cov <- matrix(
  rgamma(n_genes * n_types, shape = 4, rate = 0.2),
  n_genes,
  n_types,
  dimnames = list(paste0("gene_", seq_len(n_genes)), paste0("ct", seq_len(n_types)))
)
Sigma_cov <- array(
  0,
  c(n_genes, n_genes, n_types),
  dimnames = list(rownames(mu_cov), rownames(mu_cov), colnames(mu_cov))
)
for (j in seq_len(n_types)) {
  loadings <- matrix(rnorm(n_genes^2, sd = 0.3), n_genes)
  Sigma_cov[, , j] <- crossprod(loadings) + diag(n_genes)
}
p_true <- c(ct1 = 0.85, ct2 = 0.12, ct3 = 0.03)
bulk <- simulate_bulk_mixture(mu_cov, Sigma_cov, p = p_true, n = n_rep)$Y
fit_cov <- fit_decovart(mu_cov, bulk, Sigma = Sigma_cov, itmax = 200)
p_hat <- coef(fit_cov)

z_crit <- qnorm(0.975)
interval_routes <- function(p, n_draws = 2000L) {
  rho <- isometric_log_ratio(p)
  jac <- jacobian_isometric_logistic(rho)
  info_rho <- t(jac) %*%
    expected_fisher_unconstrained(p, mu_cov, Sigma_cov) %*%
    jac
  vcov_rho <- solve(info_rho)
  se_p <- sqrt(diag(jac %*% vcov_rho %*% t(jac)))
  draws <- MASS::mvrnorm(n_draws, rho, vcov_rho)
  p_draws <- t(apply(draws, 1L, isometric_logistic))
  list(
    delta = cbind(p - z_crit * se_p, p + z_crit * se_p),
    back_transformed = t(
      apply(p_draws, 2L, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
    )
  )
}

# Both routes need an interior estimate: on a face the ILR chart
# diverges and the information in rho is singular.
interior <- apply(p_hat, 2L, min) > 1e-6
routes <- lapply(which(interior), function(i) interval_routes(p_hat[, i]))

summarise_route <- function(name) {
  lower <- sapply(routes, function(r) r[[name]][, 1])
  upper <- sapply(routes, function(r) r[[name]][, 2])
  data.frame(
    route = name,
    cell_type = names(p_true),
    coverage = rowMeans(lower <= p_true & p_true <= upper),
    outside_unit_interval = rowMeans(lower < 0 | upper > 1),
    median_width = apply(upper - lower, 1L, median)
  )
}
route_summary <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c("delta", "back_transformed"), summarise_route)
)
rownames(route_summary) <- NULL
knitr::kable(route_summary, digits = 3)
```

Out of `r n_rep` fits, `r n_rep - sum(interior)` returned an estimate on
a simplex face, where neither route is defined; the table is computed on
the `r sum(interior)` interior fits. Three readings follow.

- The delta method places
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * route_summary$outside_unit_interval[route_summary$route == "delta" & route_summary$cell_type == "ct3"])`
  of the intervals for the rare type partly below zero. Truncating them
  at zero would hide, not fix, the problem.
- The back-transformed intervals never leave $(0,1)$ and are wider for
  the rare type, as an asymmetric interval should be.
- Neither route is calibrated for every type, and they miss in opposite
  directions. The delta method reaches its nominal coverage only by
  spending most of the rare-type interval on negative proportions; the
  back-transformed route covers the abundant type in
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * route_summary$coverage[route_summary$route == "back_transformed" & route_summary$cell_type == "ct1"])`
  of the fits. The normal approximation of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ is the
  weak link, and the routes only change how its error is mapped to the
  simplex.

The delta method on $\boldsymbol{p}$ is therefore defensible only for
balanced mixtures with few types, where every $\hat p_j$ is far from
zero. Otherwise report the back-transformed interval, or the profile
interval of @sec-interior, which needs no normal approximation of
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ at all.

## Nuisance scales: profile likelihood and orthogonality {#sec-nuisance}

In @eq-final-model the scales $\boldsymbol{\eta}=(\log c_i,\log\phi_i)$ are
technical nuisance parameters and $\boldsymbol{\rho}_i$ is the parameter of
interest. Concentrating them out gives the profile log-likelihood
$\ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho})=\ell(\boldsymbol{\rho},\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}(\boldsymbol{\rho}))$.

::: {#def-envelope}
## Envelope theorem

Let $\ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho})=\max_{\boldsymbol{\eta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{\rho},\boldsymbol{\eta})$
with a differentiable maximiser $\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}(\boldsymbol{\rho})$. Then

$$
\nabla\ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho})
=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\ell(\boldsymbol{\rho},\boldsymbol{\eta})
\big\rvert_{\boldsymbol{\eta}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}(\boldsymbol{\rho})},
$$ {#eq-envelope}

because the chain-rule term
$\{\partial\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}/\partial\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\top}\}^{\top}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\eta}}\ell$
vanishes where $\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\eta}}\ell=\boldsymbol{0}$.
:::

@eq-envelope is how the profile score of the single-cell model is
obtained without differentiating the closed-form $\hat c(\boldsymbol{p})$ and
$\hat\phi(\boldsymbol{p})$. Differentiating once more, and using
$\partial\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}/\partial\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\top}=-\boldsymbol{j}_{\eta\eta}^{-1}\boldsymbol{j}_{\eta\rho}$
from the implicit function theorem, gives the Schur complement

$$
-\nabla^{2}\ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho})
=\boldsymbol{j}_{\rho\rho}-\boldsymbol{j}_{\rho\eta}\boldsymbol{j}_{\eta\eta}^{-1}\boldsymbol{j}_{\eta\rho},
$$ {#eq-profile-schur}

so profile and joint Wald intervals for $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ agree, and
estimating the scales widens them by the loss of
[the Schur-complement information](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#eq-schur-information).

**Orthogonality.** @coxParameterOrthogonalityApproximate1987 call
$\boldsymbol{\rho}$ and $\boldsymbol{\eta}$ orthogonal when the cross block of the
expected information vanishes, $I_{\rho\eta}=\boldsymbol{0}$, so that the
information is block diagonal. Orthogonality implies that
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}$ are asymptotically independent,
that the standard error of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ is the same whether
$\boldsymbol{\eta}$ is known or estimated, and that $\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{\tau}$
varies only by $O_P(N^{-1})$ with $\tau$ (their Sect. 2.2). In a
generalised linear model the dispersion is orthogonal to the mean
parameters (their Sect. 3.2), which is why a GLM interval for the
coefficients does not depend on how the dispersion is estimated.

The single-cell model is only partly orthogonal: $I_{c\phi}=0$, but
$I_{p_jc}=c\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}/\phi\neq0$
and $I_{p_j\phi}=\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j})/(2\phi)\neq0$,
with $\boldsymbol{W}=\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})^{-1}$. The block structure is
derived for every alignment strategy in the
[single-cell vignette](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-compound).
A scalar interest parameter can always be made orthogonal to the
nuisance by solving a system of partial differential equations, whereas
a vector one in general cannot (their Sect. 2.3), so orthogonalising
the whole of $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ is not available in general. With
orthogonal nuisance parameters, the Cox--Reid adjusted profile
log-likelihood

$$
\ell_{\mathrm{CR}}(\tau)=\ell^{\ast}(\tau)
-\tfrac12\log\det\boldsymbol{j}_{\eta\eta}(\tau,\hat{\boldsymbol{\eta}}_{\tau})
$$ {#eq-cox-reid}

corrects the profile for the estimation of $\boldsymbol{\eta}$, as restricted
maximum likelihood does for a variance. The
[plug-in strategy](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-strategy-plugin)
is the opposite choice: fix the scales from external data and accept the
variance correction that propagating their uncertainty requires.

## Higher-order likelihood asymptotics {#sec-higher-order}

The first-order statistics have errors $r\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)+O(n^{-1/2})$
and $\mathcal{D}\sim\chi^{2}_k+O(n^{-1})$. Here $n$ is not necessarily a sample
size: "it can also be another parameter of the likelihood that controls
the convergence of the likelihood to the asymptotic limit"
[@canoneroHigherorderAsymptoticCorrections2023, p. 3], which for
DeCovarT is the number of replicates $N$ or the number of cells $n_i$
(@sec-regularity). Two corrections reduce the error when $n$ is small or
the log-likelihood is far from quadratic.

- **Modified likelihood root.** $r^{\ast}=r+r^{-1}\log(\upsilon/r)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)+O(n^{-3/2})$,
  where $\upsilon$ is built from sample-space derivatives of $\ell$ at the
  unrestricted and restricted estimates, with a nuisance adjustment
  $\{\det\boldsymbol{j}_{\tau\tau}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\vartheta}})/\det\boldsymbol{j}_{\eta\eta}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\vartheta}}_0)\}^{1/2}$,
  or from a tangent exponential model when $\ell$ cannot be written as a
  function of the estimates. It needs a scalar interest parameter and,
  like $r$, keeps a sign, so it gives lower and upper limits.
- **Bartlett correction.** $\mathcal{D}^{\ast}=k\mathcal{D}/\mathbb{E}(\mathcal{D})$ matches the mean of
  $\chi^{2}_k$, and the error of the $\chi^{2}_k$ approximation falls to
  $O(n^{-2})$. $\mathbb{E}(\mathcal{D})$ comes from Lawley's expansion or from a
  parametric bootstrap at the restricted estimate.

Both corrections give intervals by the inversion of @sec-test-inversion.
In the comparison of @canoneroHigherorderAsymptoticCorrections2023, the
Bartlett correction was the more reliable: $r^{\ast}$ became numerically
unstable when the log-likelihood was strongly non-Gaussian (their pp. 11
and 17). For DeCovarT, the restricted simulations of
[`bootstrap_decovart()`](../reference/bootstrap_decovart.html) already
estimate $\mathbb{E}(\mathcal{D})$, so the Bartlett factor costs no extra fit, and
`likelihoodAsy::rstar()` needs only the log-likelihood and
`simulate_bulk_mixture()`. Neither correction applies at a face, where
the problem is not regular (@sec-boundary). The Cox--Reid adjustment of
@eq-cox-reid is the third higher-order device, aimed at the nuisance
parameters rather than at the tail of the statistic.

## Firth penalisation and finite-sample corrections {#sec-firth}

Two finite-sample problems remain: the $O(N^{-1})$ bias of the MLE
(@sec-finite-sample), and estimates that run to a face because the
likelihood is flat there. Firth's adjustment addresses both. It
maximises

$\ell_{\mathrm{F}}(\boldsymbol{\vartheta})=\ell(\boldsymbol{\vartheta})+\tfrac12\log\det I(\boldsymbol{\vartheta})$
[@firthBiasReductionMaximum1993]. With [the general Fisher information](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#eq-fisher-general) the
adjusted score is

$$
\frac{\partial\ell_{\mathrm{F}}}{\partial\vartheta_q}
=\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\vartheta_q}
+\tfrac12\,\mathrm{tr}\Bigl(I(\boldsymbol{\vartheta})^{-1}\frac{\partial I(\boldsymbol{\vartheta})}{\partial\vartheta_q}\Bigr).
$$ {#eq-persp-firth-score}

For the cell-count model of [independent cells, linear covariance](02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-cc-linear) the information depends on
$\boldsymbol{m}$ only through $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$, and
$\partial\boldsymbol{\Omega}/\partial m_q=-\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,q}\boldsymbol{\Omega}$,
so

$$
\frac{\partial I(\boldsymbol{m})_{kl}}{\partial m_q}
=-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot k}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,q}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot l}
-\mathrm{tr}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,k}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,q}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,l}\bigr),
$$ {#eq-persp-firth-dI}

where the two trace terms of the product rule coincide by
transposition and cyclicity. Both summands are negative semidefinite
contributions: information about counts **decreases** as counts grow,
because more cells inflate $\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{m})$ and deflate
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}$. Jeffreys' prior $\sqrt{\det I}$ therefore favours
small totals, and the Firth penalty on the cell-count chart pulls
$\hat n_i$ downward. That is a prior statement, not a proven bias
reduction: Firth's exact removal of the $O(N^{-1})$ term holds for the
canonical parameter of a full exponential family, whereas a Gaussian
whose mean and covariance both depend on $\boldsymbol{\vartheta}$ is a
curved family, where the Jeffreys penalty is one of several
bias-reducing modified scores and does not cancel the first-order
bias exactly. On the simplex chart of Strategy 2 the same
derivative applies to the $\boldsymbol{p}$ block with the scales $c_i$ and $\phi_i$ fixed, and
the collapse of $\det I$ near faces and under collinear signatures is
the regularising effect already argued in the perspectives vignette.
A simulation under the ADEMP template of the
[synthetic-scenarios vignette](04-1-synthetic-scenarios.html)
is the only way to decide whether the pull is a correction or a bias.

`DECALS` corrects a different estimator. Its moment regression
estimates the type-level covariances from residuals computed with
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}_i$ instead of $\boldsymbol{\pi}_i$, and the finite-sample
gap between $\hat{\boldsymbol{H}}=[\hat\pi_{ik}^{2}]$ and
$\boldsymbol{H}=[\pi_{ik}^{2}]$ deflates the estimated covariance and the
coverage of its intervals. Proposition 1 of @caiStatisticalInferenceCelltype2024
quantifies $\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{H}}^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{H}}-\boldsymbol{H}^{\top}\boldsymbol{H}]$
and $\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{H}}-\boldsymbol{H}]$ in terms of the asymptotic
covariance $V_i$ of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}_i$ and subtracts them (their
equation 7). The DeCovarT analogue is the plug-in of estimated
covariances. If $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j}$ is the sample covariance of
$C_j$ Gaussian cells, $\nu_j=C_j-1$, then
$\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j}^{-1}]=\tfrac{\nu_j}{\nu_j-G-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}^{-1}$
for $\nu_j>G+1$: the plug-in precision is inflated by a factor that
is far from one for rare types with few cells and many genes. The
first-order correction multiplies $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{W,j}$ by
$(\nu_j-G-1)/\nu_j$; the graphical-lasso shrinkage of the
reproducibility book is the regularised alternative when
$\nu_j\le G+1$. The two corrections are complementary: Firth acts on
the likelihood geometry of the composition, the Wishart or `DECALS`
correction acts on the covariance that the likelihood plugs in. A
`DECALS`-style iteration, alternating between $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}_{\cdot i}$
and a bias-corrected $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{B,j}$ regressed on
$\hat p_{ji}^{2}$ across $N$ bulk samples, is the route to a
between-population covariance when the reference has a single
replicate.

In the $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ chart the penalty has a further effect. The
information $I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}=\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}^{\top}I(\boldsymbol{p})\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}$
inherits the factor $\mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p})$, whose determinant tends to
zero as any $p_j\to 0$, so $\tfrac12\log\det I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\to-\infty$ at
the faces. The penalised estimate is therefore always finite in
$\boldsymbol{\rho}$, and Wald-type intervals around it are always defined
(our remark; the effect on coverage has to be checked by simulation).
The penalty is the log of the Jeffreys prior, so the penalised estimate
is also a posterior mode
([Bayesian vignette](05-2-bayesian-wiener.html#sec-bw-priors)).

Both models implement the penalty.
[`fit_firth_decovart()`](../reference/fit_firth_decovart.html) adds
$\tfrac12\log\det I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ with the expected information, and
[`fit_firth_single_cell()`](../reference/fit_firth_single_cell.html)
uses the observed information of the profile log-likelihood, with the
two scales concentrated out. `confint_decovart(method = "firth")` and
`confint_single_cell(method = "firth")` report a Wald interval at the
penalised estimate, and map it through the inverse chart as well.

## The sandwich for a misspecified convolution {#sec-sandwich}

If the Gaussian convolution is wrong in its variance, for example
because counts are overdispersed or the reference covariance is
mis-estimated, the inverse information understates the variance of
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$. The Godambe sandwich
$\boldsymbol{H}^{-1}\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{H}^{-1}$, with $\boldsymbol{H}$ the
negative Hessian and $\boldsymbol{K}$ the variance of the score, corrects
this; `RNA-Sieve` uses it by default
[@erdmann-phamLikelihoodbasedDeconvolutionBulk2021]. Its difficulty
here is $\boldsymbol{K}$: one bulk column gives one score vector.

A construction that works with one column (our proposal, not
implemented) uses the sequential factorisation of the Gaussian
likelihood. With the Cholesky factor $\boldsymbol{L}(\boldsymbol{p})$ of
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})$ and
$\boldsymbol{e}=\boldsymbol{L}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})$,

$$
\ell(\boldsymbol{\rho})=\sum_{g=1}^{G}\ell_g(\boldsymbol{\rho}),
\qquad
\ell_g=-\log L_{gg}-\tfrac12e_g^{2},
$$ {#eq-sequential-loglik}

where $\ell_g$ is the log-density of $y_g$ given $y_1,\ldots,y_{g-1}$.
Under the model the scores $\nabla\ell_g$ are martingale differences, so
$\hat{\boldsymbol{K}}=\sum_g\nabla\ell_g\nabla\ell_g^{\top}$ estimates the
score variance without assuming independent genes. Two limits apply:
the decomposition depends on the gene order when the model is wrong,
and $G$ contributions to a $(J-1)\times(J-1)$ matrix are few when $G$ is
small. Combined with Firth's penalty, the robust variance of the
penalised estimate is $\boldsymbol{H}_{\mathrm{F}}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{K}}\boldsymbol{H}_{\mathrm{F}}^{-1}$.

## What conformal calibration can certify {#sec-conformal}

Burakov's chapter on logistic regression ([PDF](burakov-logistic-regression.pdf)) proposes split-conformal
intervals for a fitted probability, with the Pearson residual
$r_i=(y_i-\hat p_i)/\sqrt{\hat p_i(1-\hat p_i)}$ as nonconformity score:
fit on training data, take the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile $q$ of $|r_i|$ on a
calibration set, and report
$\hat p\pm q\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)}$, clipped to $[0,1]$ (chapter 2 of Burakov,
*Logistic Regression: From Maximum Likelihood to Machine Learning*, an
external resource, not a bibliographic entry). Split-conformal theory guarantees
marginal, finite-sample coverage of the **observed label** under
exchangeability. Here $|r|\le q$ is exactly the event that $y$ falls in
the interval, which the chapter itself calls an inappropriate target
for a probability; nothing in the construction guarantees coverage of
the true probability.

The same distinction decides what conformal calibration can do for
DeCovarT, whose target is a parameter, $\boldsymbol{p}$, not a prediction.

- **Gene-level Pearson residuals** $z=\boldsymbol{L}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})$
  calibrate predictions of expression. Genes are not exchangeable,
  being correlated by design, so no conformal guarantee follows. They
  remain a useful dispersion check: $\hat\phi=\lVert\boldsymbol{z}\rVert^{2}/(G-J+1)$
  well above one signals that the information understates the variance,
  and inflating $I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}^{-1}$ by $\hat\phi$ is the
  quasi-likelihood correction of @sec-glm.
- **Calibrating $\boldsymbol{p}$ itself** needs calibration bulks with known
  composition, such as pseudo-bulks built from held-out cells. With the
  score $s=(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}-\boldsymbol{\rho})^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{V}}^{-1}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}}-\boldsymbol{\rho})$
  and the $\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$-th smallest calibration score as
  threshold, the ellipsoid $\{s\le q\}$ mapped through
  $\boldsymbol{\psi}$ is a region inside the simplex with finite-sample
  **marginal** coverage, averaged over the pseudo-bulk generator. It
  says nothing about one given sample, and nothing about real bulk
  samples that the generator does not mimic, which cannot be checked
  because real bulk samples have no labels.

# Likelihood-ratio, boundary and resampling inference {#sec-inference}

## Where the estimate sits decides the null distribution {#sec-strata}

The admissible set is a polytope, and a composition can sit in its
interior or on a stratum of its boundary. With $J=4$ cell types
$\Delta^{3}$ is a tetrahedron whose strata are the interior, four
triangular faces, six edges and four vertices, corresponding to $q=0,1,2$
or $3$ proportions equal to zero (@fig-simplex-strata).

![Strata of the tetrahedron $\Delta^{3}$ for $J=4$ cell types. Vertices are pure populations, edges and faces are compositions with two or one absent cell types, and the interior holds compositions with every type present. Dashed lines are the edges hidden behind the far vertex `ct3`. Below each panel, $q$ counts the constraints active at the estimate and the red expression is the resulting null law of the likelihood-ratio statistic: the ordinary $\chi^2_1$ of @wilksLargeSampleDistributionLikelihood1938 in the interior, and binomially weighted chi-square mixtures on the boundary strata [@hermanDistributionLikelihoodRatio1954; @selfAsymptoticPropertiesMaximum1987].](figures/simplex_boundary_tangent_cones.png){#fig-simplex-strata width=100%}

The reason the calibration changes is geometric.
@selfAsymptoticPropertiesMaximum1987 show that the boundary problem is
asymptotically equivalent to estimating the **restricted mean** of a
single multivariate Gaussian draw: the limiting law of the normalised MLE
is the distribution of the *projection* of a Gaussian score onto the
**tangent cone** that approximates the admissible set at
$\boldsymbol{p}_0$. In the interior that cone is the whole of
$\mathbb{R}^{J-1}$ and the projection is the identity, recovering
classical theory; at a face it is a half-space, at an edge a
two-dimensional wedge, and at a vertex a simplicial cone. A visual
introduction to tangent and normal cones is available in these
[ESIEE optimisation notes](https://perso.esiee.fr/~chierchg/optimization/content/05/normal_cone.html).

## Interior nulls: Wald and profile likelihood {#sec-interior}

For an interior null $H_0:p_j=c$ with $0<c<1$, two statistics are
available.

The **Wald** statistic is the cheap one:
$(\hat{p}_j-c)/\mathrm{SE}_j$ with $\mathrm{SE}_j$ the delta-method
standard error of [`vcov_ilr_delta()`](../reference/vcov_ilr_delta.html),
giving the symmetric interval of
[`confint.decovart_fit()`](../reference/fit_decovart.html). It costs one
matrix inversion, but it linearises the isometric log-ratio chart at
$\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$ [@oehlertNoteDeltaMethod1992] and is therefore
*not* invariant to reparametrisation and can place limits outside
$[0,1]$.

The Wald statistic also fails non-monotonically near a boundary. As the
estimate moves away from the null, the statistic can shrink towards
zero, which is the Hauck–Donner effect [@yeeHauckDonnerEffectWald2022].
The effect corresponds to estimates near the boundary of the parameter
space, and @yeeHauckDonnerEffectWald2022 shows it is detected by
comparing pairwise ratios of Wald, score and likelihood-ratio
statistics. So a large $p$-value from a near-simplex-vertex Wald test
can be an artefact, not evidence for the null. Use the profile
likelihood-ratio statistic below in that regime.

The **profile likelihood-ratio** statistic

$$
D_j(c)
=
2\bigl\{
  \ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})
  -
  \max_{\boldsymbol{p}\in\Delta^{J-1},\,p_j=c}\ell(\boldsymbol{p})
\bigr\}
\ \rightsquigarrow\ \chi^{2}_{1}
$$ {#eq-lrt}

concentrates out the other $J-2$ proportions instead. Because a smooth
bijection leaves likelihood ratios unchanged, @eq-lrt needs **no** delta
method and respects the simplex automatically. Inverting it gives the
asymmetric intervals of
[`confint_profile_decovart()`](../reference/confint_profile_decovart.html).

```{r}
#| label: interior-inference
signature <- matrix(
  c(20, 40, 15, 40, 20, 25, 25, 30, 35),
  nrow = 3,
  dimnames = list(paste0("gene_", 1:3), paste0("ct", 1:3))
)
Sigma <- array(
  0,
  dim = c(3, 3, 3),
  dimnames = list(
    rownames(signature),
    rownames(signature),
    colnames(signature)
  )
)
for (j in 1:3) {
  Sigma[, , j] <- diag(3) * c(1, 1.5, 1.2)[j]
}

# Eight technical replicates of ONE composition, so the asymptotics of
# Sec. 2.4 are taken in a meaningful direction.
set.seed(11)
replicates <- simulate_bulk_mixture(
  signature_matrix = signature,
  Sigma = Sigma,
  p = c(0.45, 0.35, 0.20),
  n = 8
)$Y

round(
  confint_profile_decovart(
    y = replicates,
    mean_signature_matrix = signature,
    Sigma = Sigma
  ),
  4
)
```

```{r}
#| label: interior-lrt
lrt_decovart(
  y = replicates,
  mean_signature_matrix = signature,
  Sigma = Sigma,
  null_value = c(ct1 = 0.30)
)
```

## Boundary nulls: chi-bar-square mixtures {#sec-boundary}

The scientifically interesting null is usually **absence**:
$H_0:p_j=0$ against $H_1:p_j\ge 0$. Here the parameter may move away from
the null in one direction only, so the local parameter space is a
half-line rather than a vector space, and Wilks' theorem does not apply.

::: {#thm-chibar}
## Boundary calibration

With $q$ constraints active on the boundary and $t$ interior constraints
tested simultaneously, and the corresponding information block
orthogonal to the nuisance block,

$$
\mathcal{D}
\ \rightsquigarrow\
\bar{\chi}^{2}
=
\sum_{u=0}^{q}
\binom{q}{u}2^{-q}\,
\chi^{2}_{t+u},
$$ {#eq-chibar}

where $\chi^{2}_{0}$ denotes a point mass at zero
[@selfAsymptoticPropertiesMaximum1987, Case 9]. For a single active
constraint this is the $\tfrac{1}{2}\chi^{2}_{0}+\tfrac{1}{2}\chi^{2}_{1}$
law of @hermanDistributionLikelihoodRatio1954, so the correct one-sided
p-value is $\tfrac{1}{2}\Pr(\chi^{2}_{1}>\mathcal{D})$ — **half** the naive value.
:::

[`chi_bar_square_pvalue()`](../reference/chi_bar_square_pvalue.html)
evaluates @eq-chibar, and
[`lrt_decovart()`](../reference/lrt_decovart.html) selects it
automatically when a tested value reaches 0 or 1.

```{r}
#| label: boundary-lrt
set.seed(11)
replicates_absent <- simulate_bulk_mixture(
  signature_matrix = signature,
  Sigma = Sigma,
  p = c(0.5, 0.5, 0),
  n = 8
)$Y

lrt_decovart(
  y = replicates_absent,
  mean_signature_matrix = signature,
  Sigma = Sigma,
  null_value = c(ct3 = 0)
)
```

::: {#nte-chibar-caveats .callout-warning}
## Three caveats on @eq-chibar

1. **Binomial weights are conditional.** They require the active block of
   the information matrix to be orthogonal to the nuisance block. When
   several absent cell types share signal, the mixing weights depend on
   the geometry of the tangent cone; @selfAsymptoticPropertiesMaximum1987
   exhibit a configuration (their Case 8, a *nuisance* parameter on the
   boundary) whose limit is not a chi-square mixture at all. Pass explicit
   `weights`, or calibrate by simulation (@sec-bootstrap).
2. **Do not encode the null in ILR coordinates.** $p_j=0$ corresponds to
   an infinite log-ratio, so the chart cannot represent the hypothesis. The
   restricted fits substitute the constrained value directly.
3. **Wald is unusable here.** The delta-method covariance is undefined on
   the face, and the Hauck–Donner effect
   [@yeeHauckDonnerEffectWald2022] makes its test unreliable as the
   estimate approaches it; `vcov_ilr_delta()` returns `NA` with a warning rather than a
   plausible-looking number.
:::

## Replication is what makes the asymptotics meaningful {#sec-replication}

@eq-lrt and @eq-chibar are limits as the amount of information about
**one** composition grows. That is a strong requirement in deconvolution,
and it is the same $N\to\infty$ that turns the $O(N^{-1})$ bias of
@sec-finite-sample into consistency.

For each bulk sample $i$, DeCovarT observes a single $G$-vector
$\boldsymbol{Y}_{\cdot i}\sim\mathcal{N}_G(\boldsymbol{\mu}
\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}))$
and estimates its own $\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$. Increasing the number
of samples $N$ therefore adds parameters exactly as fast as
observations, and provides **no** extra replication for any single
$\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i}$. The $G$ genes are not $G$ independent
observations either: their dependence through
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p})$ is the whole point of the model.

::: {#nte-replication .callout-important}
## Per-sample intervals are plug-in approximations

The default per-sample `vcov` and `confint` of a `decovart_fit` are
one-observation plug-in quantities. Treat them as descriptive curvature
summaries, not as calibrated frequentist intervals.

Two things restore the asymptotics, and both are implemented:

- **Pool genuine replicates.** Supply several bulk columns that really
  do share one composition (technical replicates, or aliquots of one
  tissue) as the columns of the `y` matrix of
  `lrt_decovart()` / `confint_profile_decovart()`. Those functions
  maximise the *summed* log-likelihood over the replicates, so the
  limit is taken in the number of replicates.
- **Simulate instead of appealing to a limit** (@sec-bootstrap).

Reference uncertainty is a third, separate gap: $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ are plug-in estimates from purified populations,
and none of the intervals above propagate their sampling variability.
[`reference_bootstrap_decovart()`](../reference/reference_bootstrap_decovart.html)
resamples those profiles (@sec-reference-bootstrap); see
@vellameUncertaintyQuantificationReferencebased2023 for the analogous
accuracy metric in methylation deconvolution.
:::

## Parametric bootstrap calibration {#sec-bootstrap}

The conditional law of the bulk profile is fully specified, so the
asymptotic mixture can be replaced by simulation.
[`bootstrap_decovart()`](../reference/bootstrap_decovart.html) draws
$\boldsymbol{Y}^{(b)}\sim\mathcal{N}_G(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p},
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(\boldsymbol{p}))$, refits, and — when `null_value` is
supplied — regenerates under the **restricted** MLE so the
likelihood-ratio statistic is recalibrated without invoking the
$50{:}50$ weights [@rochModernDiscreteProbability2024 reviews the
concentration tools behind such Monte Carlo guarantees].

The atom at zero is directly observable: under a true boundary null,
about half of the replicates should return $\mathcal{D}=0$, because the
unrestricted MLE itself falls on the face.

```{r}
#| label: bootstrap-calibration
set.seed(5)
calibration <- bootstrap_decovart(
  y = replicates_absent,
  mean_signature_matrix = signature,
  Sigma = Sigma,
  null_value = c(ct3 = 0),
  n_boot = 150
)
c(
  observed_statistic = calibration$statistic,
  monte_carlo_p = calibration$p_value,
  share_of_zero_statistics = mean(calibration$null_statistics < 1e-8),
  asymptotic_p = chi_bar_square_pvalue(
    calibration$statistic,
    n_boundary = 1L
  )
)
```

The observed share of zero statistics is the empirical counterpart of the
$\tfrac{1}{2}\chi^{2}_{0}$ atom in @eq-chibar. A restricted bootstrap is
still only *approximate* for a composite null, because the nuisance
proportions are held at their restricted estimates rather than profiled
over; it is exact only when $\boldsymbol{p}_0$ is fully specified.

## Reference-sample bootstrap {#sec-reference-bootstrap}

[`bootstrap_decovart()`](../reference/bootstrap_decovart.html) treats
$\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j$ as known. They are not:
both are estimated from purified profiles.
[`reference_bootstrap_decovart()`](../reference/reference_bootstrap_decovart.html)
resamples the **experimental units of that labelled reference**, rebuilds
the plug-in moments, and refits, so reference uncertainty appears in the
percentile intervals [@efronBootstrapMethodsAnother1979]. Cell-type names
stay attached throughout. The two `method` options are:

- **`donors`** (default). Cluster bootstrap of donors *within each cell
  type*. A donor drawn twice contributes its purified columns twice.
  This is the favoured option when donor labels exist: it captures
  biological variation in the reference population rather than treating
  cells from one individual as independent.
- **`cells`**. Column resampling within each cell type, for when donor
  labels are unavailable.[^dirichlet-sweep]

[^dirichlet-sweep]: An earlier version also offered
    `method = "dirichlet"`, which drew compositions from a Dirichlet law,
    simulated bulks at the plug-in moments and refitted. It measured
    performance across random mixtures, not uncertainty for one observed
    bulk, and was removed; the effect of compositional imbalance on the
    width of the intervals is studied in the simulation scenarios
    instead.

Both options draw **with** replacement, which makes them bootstraps. A
permutation (Monte Carlo randomisation) test draws **without**
replacement: it shuffles labels to build the distribution of a statistic
under a null of exchangeability, and serves hypothesis testing rather
than interval estimation. Shuffling cell-type labels is vacuous here,
because the likelihood is equivariant under relabelling
(`equivariance_check_decovart()` below).

By default the observed bulk is held fixed (reference uncertainty for a
given mixture). Setting
`regenerate_bulk = TRUE` follows the fuller pipeline
$\text{reference units}\to S^{(b)}\to Y^{(b)}\to\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}^{(b)}$.

A related design point for **simulation studies**, not implemented as an
argument here, is to split reference-building cells from
pseudobulk-generating cells, ideally at the donor level. Using the same
cells, or cells from the same individual, in both the signature and the
artificial bulk makes a benchmark unrealistically easy
[@sturmComprehensiveEvaluationTranscriptomebased2019;
@avilacobosBenchmarkingCellType2020;
@zhaoEvaluatingReferencemixtureMatching2026].
@nguyenFourteenYearsCellular2024 review 53 bulk methods and
stress incomplete references and missing cell types; @avilacobosBenchmarkingCellType2020
show that omitted types and the expression scale dominate error on
pseudobulk mixtures. The simulation generator used to evaluate `imply`
is a useful reference-based template: cell-type parameters are drawn
from a multivariate Gaussian, purified-like expression is realised from
a Gamma (negative-binomial-like) law fitted to RNA-seq counts, and bulk
mixtures are then formed from those profiles with Dirichlet
compositions [@mengImplyImprovingCelltype2024]. That is distinct from
DeCovarT's Gaussian convolution of the *bulk*; it is a design for how to
build a labelled $S$ and a synthetic $Y$ with known $p$.

```{r}
#| label: reference-bootstrap
set.seed(9)
refs <- lapply(seq_len(ncol(signature)), function(j) {
  draws <- MASS::mvrnorm(
    n = 12L,
    mu = signature[, j],
    Sigma = Sigma[, , j]
  )
  out <- t(draws)
  rownames(out) <- rownames(signature)
  out
})
names(refs) <- colnames(signature)
donor_ids <- lapply(refs, function(x) {
  rep(paste0("d", 1:3), length.out = ncol(x))
})
ref_boot <- reference_bootstrap_decovart(
  y = replicates,
  reference_profiles = refs,
  donor_ids = donor_ids,
  method = "donors",
  n_boot = 40,
  itmax = 80
)
ref_boot$interval
```

[`equivariance_check_decovart()`](../reference/equivariance_check_decovart.html)
is a software check of label equivariance: permute the
signature columns, refit, and confirm that $\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}$ merely
relabels. It is not the distribution used for confidence intervals.

```{r}
#| label: equivariance-check
eq_check <- equivariance_check_decovart(
  y = replicates[, 1],
  mean_signature_matrix = signature,
  Sigma = Sigma,
  perm = c(3L, 1L, 2L),
  itmax = 80
)
c(
  max_abs_diff = eq_check$max_abs_diff,
  loglik_diff = eq_check$loglik_diff
)
```

## RNA-Sieve: CLT likelihood, Fisher and Godambe {#sec-rna-sieve}

`RNA-Sieve` [@erdmann-phamLikelihoodbasedDeconvolutionBulk2021], with
its gene-wise central-limit likelihood, its errors-in-variables
reference and its Fisher and Godambe intervals, is compared with
DeCovarT in the
[distribution-aware deconvolution review](05-1-review-distribution-aware.html#sec-rnasieve).

# Convergence and boundary diagnostics {#sec-diagnostics}

Because @nte-nonconcave rules out global guarantees, a single optimiser
return code carries less information than it appears to.
[`fit_decovart()`](../reference/fit_decovart.html) therefore records
three logically distinct claims, and refuses to conflate them:

| Field | Established by | Does **not** establish |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `converged` (`iterations`, `criterion`, `code`, `rdm`) | numerical stopping rules met (iterative solvers; `NA` for NNLS / LSEI / CIBERSORT) | that the point is a maximum |
| `local_maximum` (small ILR score, $\lambda_{\min}(H_z)<0$ and $\lambda_{\max}(H_z)<0$) | stationarity with a negative-definite Hessian | global optimality |
| `near_boundary` ($\min_j\hat{p}_j$ small) | proximity to a simplex face | optimiser failure |
| `multimodal` (spread of log-likelihoods over random starts) | evidence *for* several modes | absence of further modes |

: What each DeCovarT convergence field does and does not certify. {#tbl-diagnostics}

[`boundary_diagnostics()`](../reference/boundary_diagnostics.html)
computes the first three per sample; they are stored in
`fit$diagnostics`.

```{r}
#| label: diagnostics
fit <- fit_decovart(
  signature_matrix = signature,
  bulk_expression = replicates[, 1:3],
  Sigma = Sigma,
  itmax = 100
)
do.call(rbind, fit$diagnostics)
```

Every sample above converged and every curvature is negative, yet
`local_maximum` is not uniformly `TRUE`: one iterate stopped with an ILR
score norm just above the default `score_tol = 1e-4`. That is the
distinction of @tbl-diagnostics doing its job rather than a failure —
`score_tol` bounds the *score*, whereas the solver's `epsilon` bounds the
*objective*, so the two should be tightened together.

::: {#nte-boundary-wording .callout-note}
## Near-boundary is not failure

Suppose the truth is $\boldsymbol{p}_0=(0,0.3,0.7)$. A fit returning
$\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}=(10^{-10},0.3001,0.6999)$ is numerically
*excellent*: the optimiser is correctly approaching a genuine boundary
optimum, and an interior ILR solver cannot settle at a finite
$\boldsymbol{z}$ there. So $\min_j\hat{p}_j\ll 1$ should not be read
as "optimisation failed" but as

> the estimate is close to a simplex face, so ILR coordinates and
> interior Wald inference may be unreliable.
